turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Ken, arm down when you're ready. Blood pressure is 152 over 88, pulse 74, oxygen 97 percent. The letter on file lists perindopril 4 milligrams each morning.

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): 152? That cuff's having a lend of me. The chemist last Tuesday, young bloke with the earring, got a much kinder number, and I've been off the chips since bowls started back. Perindopril, yes, the little white one, I've swallowed that for years, ever since the blood pressure fuss.

[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The home machine said about 140 on 80 this morning, but that's not the point of today, and that letter's stale. Perindopril is 8 milligrams, Dr Shah put it up, I want to say last August, though don't quote me on the month. I pack the Webster myself.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): I'll leave the dose for the doctor, the file still says 4. She's free, room two.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Come in, Ken. Pat, thanks for bringing him. I'm Dr Ellison. The booking says memory, but I'd rather you tell it, Pat, in ordinary words.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll say he's fine. He repeats questions, he forgets appointments, and last week he got lost at the shops. That's why I rang.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): I am fine. I'm seventy-nine, not ninety, and I don't forget appointments. They go in the blue diary by the phone, not the red one, the red one's bowls, and I read it out after the news so there's no mystery.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): The repeating questions, Pat. How long has that actually been going?
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Eighteen months, easy. Most days. What time are we going, again and again, right up to the door.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Eighteen months is a story. Two or three months, since the bowls finals, and it's twice, not a dozen times, because the telly's loud and I like to be sure. I've always double-checked things, even the timesheets at the council, that's just me.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): So I'm hearing anywhere from a few months to a year and a half, and you don't agree. I won't nail a number down today. The repeating itself, you both accept it happens.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ken, at the shops, did you get lost?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I didn't get lost. I knew exactly where I was. Westfield, level two, the Coles end, I've used that car park since they opened it, I could draw you the arrows.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Security rang me. He was gone nearly an hour. Couldn't find the car, then couldn't find the way out. They walked him to the boom gate.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any falls lately?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No falls. Not a one. I watch the back step, the brick sits proud, and I've been meaning to ring a brickie, it's our house, we own it, no landlord, I misspoke just then.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Have you been more tired?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. The lawn still gets done, I just stop for a second cuppa halfway, Bushells, nothing fancy.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): I won't put tiredness down off a suppose. Any chest pain, or trouble breathing?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. Breathing's fine. The hill up to the oval puffs me, but that hill's been steep since the reseal, years back, nothing to do with this.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He missed the podiatrist last month and the eye check in March. Both were written on the fridge. He told me he'd gone.

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I did not miss them. Podiatry cancelled, the girl with the headset said the podiatrist was crook, and at the eye place I sat in the blue chairs and they couldn't find the file, so they sent me home. That's their mess, not a forgotten appointment.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can't tell which of those is true from here. Missed, cancelled, lost file. I'm leaving the appointments as something you two dispute.
[SEG0024] person_4 (DOCTOR): How's sleep, and appetite?

[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Sleep's ordinary. I wake around two for the toilet, have done for donkey's years, then I read a bit of that cricket biography and I'm off. Appetite's good. Toast, vegemite, two slices, most mornings.
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The night toilet thing is fair, it's been years. Eating's been normal. I'm not here about food.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Who handles the tablets?

[SEG0028] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I do. Webster pack, Sundays. Morning is perindopril 8 milligrams for the blood pressure, plus aspirin 100 milligrams, the Cartia. Night is atorvastatin 40 milligrams for the cholesterol.

[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I take whatever's in the little compartments and I don't tip them out, she gets snaky. There is a green capsule at night. She told me the name once. It went straight through, names do that, they always have, even the street names when I was on the truck.

[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The green one is the atorvastatin, the 40. Thing is, last Thursday the night slots still had the tablets in. I was at bingo. So I'm not sure he took them. Mornings I'm watching, those are gone.

[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thinking it through, I'll take atorvastatin as 40 at night, but if the pack still had tablets then adherence on that night dose is doubtful. Perindopril stays dose-unknown for me, file 4 versus your 8, until we see Shah's letter. Aspirin 100 in the morning is the clear one. I won't change any of them today.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Someone definitely said go up to the higher perindopril. Shah, or the locum with the beard who did the Friday clinic. The chemist box just says one daily. White packet, blue writing, second shelf at Chemist Warehouse, I can see it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure and cholesterol, they're already the longstanding problems, still current?
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Both still going, years. No diabetes. He doesn't smoke, he quit before I even met him, and he barely drinks, a light beer at bowls if he bothers.

[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Last cigarette was 1989, the week our eldest went into the army, I remember the brand I threw out, Winfield red. One beer, sometimes none, the new tap beer tastes like soap. I walk most days, three blocks past the servo, if the knee's in the mood, which it usually is.
[SEG0036] person_4 (DOCTOR): I won't open up allergies or the family history today, there isn't time, and I'm not marching through every body system. I do want a quick look at you, Ken.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Allergies, well, nobody's asked me that in ages, and I was going to tell you about the lawnmower fuel anyway. Two-stroke, I mix it myself, forty to one, which is fiddly with these fingers.
[SEG0038] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hands out for me. Grip's the same both sides. No swelling at the ankles. Heart sounds are regular with no murmur, and the chest is clear.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): You had the day of the week and you knew the suburb straight off. I'm not putting you through a long memory test in the room.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He can do the day. It's new things that fall out. And he waved me off before, so I'll say the shops bit again. It was last Thursday arvo.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, I'll say it properly. I came off level two and the car wasn't where I thought, so I looped past the chemist, the food court and the travelator, and I could not find the exit sign I always use. A security bloke in a blue shirt took me to the boom gate, so yes, I was turned around, annoyed more than scared, and I still knew where Coles was. Call it twenty minutes, I wasn't clock-watching.
[SEG0042] person_4 (DOCTOR): So last Thursday you were lost in that car park, somewhere between twenty minutes and the hour Pat said. I'm not putting a name on it.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty minutes. I'll stick. And I bought the milk on the way, full cream, two litres, so the trip wasn't a waste, we were out of milk for the tea.
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was an hour. Security rang at ten past four and he'd headed off at about ten to three. I looked at the clock because the roast was in.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Home together, just the two of you?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Just us, since Molly died in June, the kelpie, I still hang the lead on the hook which is silly, I know. Pat cooks. I do the bins and the lawn. No one else stays.

[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking this might be nothing dramatic, or it might be something we ought to chase, and I am not going to say which today. Bloods and a proper memory assessment will tell us more than a guess will.
[SEG0048] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): What are you actually booking?

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pathology this week, I'll order a full blood count, kidney function, thyroid, B12 and folate, and a fasting glucose. And I'll refer you to the memory clinic for a memory assessment, the longer testing. No new tablet, nothing stopped.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting means no toast that morning, I get it, even though vegemite on wholemeal is half my personality. Will those memory people try to catch me out? I used to do the timesheets to the cent, I don't fancy looking foolish in front of a stranger.

[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): No trick questions, just a proper look at memory. Come back and see me in four weeks, results or not. If you get lost again before that, don't sit on it, ring and we'll see you sooner.
[SEG0052] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll bring the Webster pack and Shah's letter so the 8 milligrams can be checked. And I'll come to the clinic with him.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do. Ken, stick with Pat for the shops for now, and keep taking what's in the pack instead of tipping them out to inspect. We'll go through it all in four weeks.

spec.situation: Spouse brings an older person who 'is fine' but repeats questions, forgets appointments and got lost; patient disagrees on many points; medicines managed by spouse; doctor plans bloods and a memory assessment, no diagnosis said aloud.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
